title: French Defense: each side's setup and what each move prepares
outcomes: Says what each of White's moves c3, Nf3, Be2 and Na3-c2 prepares in the Advance, and picks the knight move (Na3, not Nbd2) that keeps the c1 bishop free and reaches c2
Counts the attackers and defenders of d4 and e5 while a setup is built, for either colour
Says what f4, Nf3 and Be3 prepare for White in the Classical setup and what ...a6 and ...Be7 prepare for Black
Recognises that two move orders can reach the same position and counts again
sources: app/public/masters/stats.json (329,379 games, both players 2,500+, 2012-2026; counts quoted from the tree) [V]
content/items/lesson-od-french-3.json (every move line replayed with python-chess; claims machine-checked, engine depth 16) [V]
content/skills/OPN.SETUP.json, OPN.STRUCT.json, POS.STRUCTURE.CHAIN.json, POS.BREAKS.json (core ideas, linked by name)
Reasons named [I]/[H] are the author's inference, not a cited theory

steps.caption: Black to move. White has made seven moves, and each one has a job. Two white pieces have not moved yet: the knight on b1 and the bishop on c1. Before you read on, ask what each is waiting for, and how safe the pawn on d4 is.

claims.statement: Three white pieces defend d4 (pawn c3, knight f3, queen d1).
Two black pieces attack d4 (pawn c5 and knight c6).
The bishop on c1 can move to five squares.

steps.chapter: A setup is a list of reasons

steps.prompt: Before reading on: what do you think the knight on b1 and the bishop on c1 are waiting for? Write a guess.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** A setup is not a list of moves; it is a list of reasons. For each side you will say what a move prepares and which move order is flexible. The tool is the same all the way through: count the attackers and the defenders of the key pawn.

steps.caption: White's first job in the Advance. Step through it and say what the pawn on c3 makes possible.

line.say: The c-pawn defends d4, so the queen is no longer the only defender.
Black trades the lever pawn for the base.
The pawn recaptures. The chain is rebuilt on d4 and e5, and Black has spent a tempo and a pawn to trade the lever for White's c-pawn.

claims.statement: After c3 two white pieces defend d4 (pawn and queen).
After the pawn recapture a white pawn defends e5 again.

steps.caption: What 5.Nf3 prepares. Count after the move.

line.say: The knight defends d4 and e5 at once. It is the third defender of d4 and the second of e5.

claims.statement: After Nf3 three white pieces defend d4.
After Nf3 two white pieces defend e5 (pawn d4 and knight f3).

steps.caption: What 6.Be2 prepares. Step through it and watch the king and the rook.

line.say: The bishop leaves f1 so the king can castle, and it stays off the d-file so the queen still guards d4.
Black develops the knight.
White castles. The king leaves the e-file and the rook reaches f1.

claims.statement: The king stands on g1 after castling.
The rook stands on f1 after castling.
After castling three white pieces still defend d4.

steps.text: **The knight on b1.** It wants to reach c2, where it will defend d4 from behind, and from b1 only the move to a3 gets there. The other natural move, to d2, develops the knight but blocks the bishop on c1 and cannot reach c2. Predict which move keeps the bishop free, then test it.

steps.caption: The knight route that keeps the bishop free. Step through it first to the pawn trade.

line.say: The knight heads for c2. It stays off the bishop's diagonal.
Black trades the c-pawn for the d-pawn.
The pawn recaptures; the c-file is open.

claims.statement: After Na3 the bishop on c1 can move to five squares.

steps.caption: A second knight attacks d4 and the white knight lands on c2. Count at the end.

line.say: A second knight attacks d4. Two black pieces now attack the base.
The knight lands on c2 and guards d4 from behind. White now has three defenders to Black's two.

claims.statement: After Nc2 three white pieces defend d4.
Two black pieces attack d4.

steps.text: **Black's setup builds the same count from the other side.** The pawn on c5 starts, the knight on c6 adds, and a knight on f5 adds a third. Watch the attackers grow as the pieces arrive.

steps.caption: Black's setup, move by move. First the second attacker, and the bishop out of the pawns' way.

line.say: The second attacker on d4. It also attacks e5.
White adds a third defender.
The bad bishop gets out of the pawns' way and leaves c8 free for a rook.

claims.statement: After ...Nc6 two black pieces attack d4.
After ...Nc6 one black piece attacks e5.

steps.caption: White develops; Black brings the knight toward f5, where it will attack d4.

line.say: White develops.
The knight heads for f5, where it will attack d4.

steps.caption: White castles. The knight arrives. Count the attackers at the end.

line.say: White castles.
The knight arrives. Three black pieces attack d4 and three white pieces defend it.

claims.statement: After ...Nf5 three black pieces attack d4.
Three white pieces defend d4.

steps.caption: Another Black setup: the queen replaces the pawn on the diagonal. Step through the first moves.

line.say: The queen stands behind the c-pawn on the diagonal toward d4 and aims at b2.
White develops.
The pawn trade opens the diagonal for the queen.

claims.statement: After ...Qb6 the queen attacks b2.

steps.caption: Count the attackers on d4 at the end. The count is 2 against 2, but it ignores what each attacker is worth: a queen is a costly piece to risk, and ...Qb6 also hits b2.

line.say: White recaptures.
The knight heads for f5 by another route.

claims.statement: At the end two black pieces attack d4 (knight c6 and queen b6).
Two white pieces defend d4 (knight f3 and queen d1).

steps.text: **What strong players chose.** In our master data (329,379 games, both players rated 2,500 or more, 2012 to 2026), 1,806 games reached the Advance, and Black played the c-pawn lever in 1,751. White then supported d4 with the pawn in 1,717; the knight came first in only 33. Black then chose the knight on c6 in 1,322 and the queen on b6 in 269. Counts of choices, not evaluations.

**A different third move.** White can also develop first and keep the pawn flexible. This is the Classical branch, the 4.e5 line (called Steinitz). After the knight on c3 and Black's knight on f6, White can push at once: the pawn attacks the knight, the knight must move, and a chain grows with a different support. Here the pawn on f4, not on c3, will prop up e5.

steps.caption: The Classical setup, move by move. Count the defenders of e5 and d4 as they grow.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight on f6 and takes space.
The knight retreats and attacks e5 at once.
A second defender of e5: pawn d4 and pawn f4.

claims.statement: After e5 a white pawn attacks f6.
After ...Nfd7 one black piece attacks e5.
After f4 two white pieces defend e5.

line.say: The lever against the base d4.
A third defender joins e5; it guards d4 too.
A second black piece attacks e5 and d4.

claims.statement: After ...Nc6 two black pieces attack e5.
After Nf3 three white pieces defend e5.

steps.caption: The bishop move you found, on the board. Count the defenders of d4 now.

line.say: A third defender of d4. Nothing needs to be added to e5 yet.

claims.statement: After Be3 three white pieces defend d4.
Two black pieces attack d4.
At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between 0 and 70 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.text: **What strong players chose.** In our master data (2,500+ rated), the pawn push came in 1,760 games after the knight on f6, and the bishop to g5 in 1,010. After the knight retreat, White played the pawn to f4 in 1,504 of 1,732. After Black's knight reached c6, the bishop to e3 came in 1,301 of 1,338. Counts of choices, not evaluations.

steps.caption: Black's moves in the Classical setup and what each prepares.

line.say: The bishop develops and prepares to castle.
White's queen stays a third guard of d4 and clears d1, so castling long is possible.
The pawn attacks b5, stopping a knight or bishop from landing there, and prepares ...b5.

claims.statement: After Qd2 three white pieces defend d4 (knight f3, bishop e3, queen d2).
After ...a6 a black pawn attacks b5.
At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between 0 and 70 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.caption: Move order. Step through it and compare the position at the end with the main line.

line.say: The knight comes first this time.
Black adds the second attacker.
White adds the pawn. This is the same position as the main line after 5.Nf3, reached by a different move order.

claims.statement: After the third white move three white pieces defend d4.
Two black pieces attack d4.

steps.text: **Why the pawn first.** [V] The two orders reach one position when Black answers the knight with ...Nc6 (replayed with python-chess). [I] Played first, the knight gives Black a choice, such as ...Qb6, before White has committed the c-pawn; the pawn first meets ...c5 at once. Masters chose the pawn first in 1,717 games and the knight first in 33. If a move order surprises you, count d4 again.

steps.prompt: [H] In the Advance White's moves mostly protect; in the Classical setup they mostly build. List one move in each set-up that protects and one that builds, and say which category f4 belongs to.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** A setup is a list of reasons. In the Advance, the c-pawn, the knight on f3 and a knight reaching c2 each add a defender to d4; the bishop on e2 prepares castling. Black adds attackers with the c-pawn, both knights and the queen. In the Classical setup the f-pawn defends e5, the knight and bishop defend d4, and Black's a-pawn prepares queenside space. Move orders can transpose: count the key pawn again.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in two or three sentences, explain to a beginner what 5.Nf3 prepares in the Advance and what the pawn on f4 prepares in the Classical setup. Say when each works and when it does not, give one example you could set up on a board, and one mistake to avoid. Self-check afterwards: did you say when it works and when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.
